title: Majestic Sacrifice
reviewNotes: Montage, captions and native complete later boards reviewed. Begin after ...Rd7 at 148 seconds in the complete eight-piece later diagram: White Kh2/c7/g2 against Kh8/Rd7/b6/f6/h7. The source c8=Q+ promotion is certified against both legal replies: Rd8 and Kg7, followed by the corresponding rook capture into an exact seven-piece win. Black replies and capture completions are explicitly independent additions to the source’s promotion diagram. Earlier eleven-piece knight sacrifices, d6 interference and other rook/knight branches remain outside proof. Native images establish c7/Rd7/Kh2, correcting earlier provisional b7/c7 and Kg2 assumptions.
transcript: Cowards will run. Warriors will stay and fight. But only a true hero will be able to prevail. You see, in this position, it seems like black is completely winning. The pawn is one step away from promoting, but the rook will always be able to stop it. And even if the knight somehow magically managed to defend the promotion square, this would still be a favorable endgame for black because this knight is more advanced and this pawn is pretty much unstoppable. But white is a true hero for a reason. And it plays knight to D6, setting up a pretty straightforward trap if black is not careful. Now, knight to C8 is going to block the vision of the rook and prepare the promotion. And this knight has no way to stop that. But black is not that naive. And it plays knight to C7. And now after knight to C8, knight E6 is going to stop the promotion and black is simply going to win. So because of that, white plays D5 covering the E6 square and preparing this idea. But black is rated 3,021 for a reason and it sees the threat. So it plays rook to F8. And now if the knight tries to go to E8, the rook is going to sacrifice itself. And after the pawn takes it, the knight is going to take and black is simply going to win. Which means that black is out of the woods and there was no hope after all. Except there is. And white plays knight to E8. Anyway, a brilliant move. First of all, if the knight takes, we simply promote. And now a queen is going to be enough to win this. But what if the rook takes? What is the continuation? We cannot promote here because the rook is going to take. And we already saw that taking the rook doesn't work. Well, the incredible move that wins for white in this position is D6. and D6 attacks the knight and leaves the attack on the rook at the same time, forcing black to make a decision. If the knight moves, of course, we're going to have a queen rising from the ashes like a phoenix. But if the rook moves and tries to stop the pawn, sacrificing the knight back, well, now the rook is overwhelmed. It cannot stop both of these pawns at the same time. And no matter what happens, one of the pawns is simply going to call back a queen from the grave. And the hero is going to rise victorious from this incredible position. If you love incredible chess, follow for more.
